planting.note: Set out plugs or divisions in spring into wet, seasonally flooded soil; fresh seed benefits from cold moist stratification if sowing rather than dividing.

directions: Ravenfoot sedge gets its common name from the spreading, claw-like perigynia clusters that ripen along its seedheads in late spring, a distinctive field mark among bottomland Carex species. It is native to floodplain forests, sloughs, and seasonally inundated bottomlands across the Gulf South and lower Mississippi valley, where it tolerates standing winter water followed by summer drawdown. In cultivation it works well at the muddy edge of a rain garden or detention basin, or scattered through wet woodland plantings, where its arching deep-green foliage provides erosion control and seed forage for waterfowl and songbirds. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes to form loose colonies rather than aggressive mats.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring into consistently moist to wet soil; seed germinates best after a period of cold moist stratification.

directions: Greenwhite sedge forms upright tufts of narrow foliage topped in late spring by pale, straw-colored seed clusters that give the plant its name, showy enough to notice against the surrounding green. It is native to wet meadows, ditches, and pond margins across the southeastern coastal plain, including the Gulf Coast, where it colonizes seasonally saturated open ground. It is a useful, low-maintenance filler for a sunny to lightly shaded rain garden or pond edge, holding soil in place with a fibrous root system while offering nesting cover and seed for marsh birds. Established clumps tolerate both standing water after storms and drier spells once roots are settled.

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in well-drained sandy or loamy soil beneath open woodland canopy; the fine hairs covering its leaves and stems help identify it from similar dry-woods Carex species.

directions: Hirsute sedge is a diminutive, clump-forming species distinguished by the fine pubescence covering its leaf sheaths and stems, unusual among Carex and a handy identification trait. Native to sandy pine woods and dry-mesic upland forests across the southeastern coastal plain into East Texas, it thrives where taller sedges struggle: dappled shade over lean, well-drained sand. Its small stature and tolerance of dry shade make it a fitting groundcover for a native pine-woodland garden alongside wildflowers like partridge pea and native asters, offering fine winter-green texture and incidental seed for small birds without requiring supplemental water once established.

planting.note: Direct sow in late spring once soil has warmed, in lean sandy or rocky, well-drained ground; this warm-season grass germinates readily without stratification but needs heat to establish.

directions: Bearded skeletongrass forms low rosettes of broad, spreading leaf blades from which wiry, widely branched flower stalks radiate in a distinctive open, skeletal pattern in late summer and fall, giving the plant its name. It is native to dry, sandy pinelands, open woods, and disused fields across the southeastern and south-central United States, including East Texas and the Gulf Coast sandhills, where it tolerates drought and infertile soil that few ornamental grasses can handle. Its unusual candelabra-like inflorescence adds sculptural interest to a native meadow planting through fall, and it provides cover and seed for ground-nesting birds and small wildlife on sites too dry and lean for turf.

planting.note: Surface-sow the fine seed on bare, lean sandy soil in spring after frost, pressing lightly rather than burying; this small pioneer sedge self-sows readily once established on open ground.

directions: Densetuft hairsedge is a wiry, thread-fine annual or short-lived perennial sedge that colonizes bare, dry, sandy or rocky open ground, from disturbed roadside cuts to sandy pine barrens, across most of the eastern and central United States including the Gulf Coast. Its tiny reddish-brown spikelets sit atop hair-like stems in loose clusters through summer, easy to overlook but ecologically valuable as an early colonizer that stabilizes bare sand ahead of other natives. It suits the leanest, driest microsites in a native seed mix, such as the gravelly margin of a path or a sun-baked sand patch, where it needs no irrigation or soil amendment and asks only for open ground free of competition.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring once soil has warmed; knotroot bristlegrass germinates quickly from fresh seed and spreads on its own from short scaly rhizomes once established.

directions: Knotroot bristlegrass is a fine-textured warm-season bunchgrass topped from summer into fall by dense, bottlebrush-like seedheads bearing the bristly awns typical of Setaria, favored by seed-eating birds like doves and sparrows. Native throughout the southern and Gulf Coast United States, it grows in open fields, roadsides, and disturbed prairies on a wide range of soils and tolerates both drought and periodic flooding. Its short, knotty rhizomes let it form loose sod useful for stabilizing bare or eroding ground in a naturalistic meadow planting, and its seed is a reliable, low-input food source through the leanest part of winter when many showier natives have gone dormant.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for a spring bloom, pressing seed onto bare soil without covering; like other native winter-annual coreopsis it germinates with cool-season rain and overwinters as a low rosette.

directions: Wright's coreopsis produces slender, wiry stems topped with yellow, red-brown-centered daisy flowers in spring, closely resembling its more widely grown relative golddust coreopsis but generally finer in habit and later to bloom. It is native to open prairies, limestone outcrops, and roadsides of the Edwards Plateau and South Texas, thriving on thin, alkaline soils that stay dry through summer. As a self-sowing winter annual, it fills bare ground with a low rosette through fall and winter before flowering en masse in spring, drawing small native bees and butterflies, then setting seed and fading with summer heat, leaving room for warm-season natives to take over.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring at the base of a fence, shrub, or trellis for the twining vine to climb; scarify seed lightly and keep soil moist until germination.

directions: Pearl milkvine produces small, star-shaped flowers with a netted, pearl-and-maroon reticulated pattern across each petal, an unusual and easily identified bloom among Texas native vines. It twines through brush and fenceline vegetation on rocky prairies, caliche flats, and open woodland edges across South and Central Texas into Mexico, tolerating heat, drought, and thin alkaline soil that few other flowering vines survive. As a member of the milkweed subfamily it exudes milky sap and serves as a larval host for queen butterflies, making it a worthwhile if slow-growing addition to a xeric native pollinator garden trained on a low trellis or allowed to scramble through companion shrubs.
